**Darius III and the Battles of Issus and Gaugamela**
Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III at Issus (333 BCE), in southern Turkey near the Pinarus River, and decisively at Gaugamela (331 BCE) in northern Mesopotamia. These victories brought down the Achaemenid Persian Empire; Darius fled and was later murdered by his satrap Bessus, whom Alexander captured and executed.

**Bucephalus**
Alexander's famous warhorse, which as a boy he tamed by turning it toward the sun so it could not see its own shadow. Bucephalus died around the time of the Battle of the Hydaspes, and Alexander founded the city of Bucephala in its honor; the horse appears in the Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii.

**Battle of the Hydaspes and King Porus**
Alexander's 326 BCE victory in Punjab over the Indian king Porus and his war elephants. Allied with the local ruler Taxiles, Alexander crossed the monsoon-swollen river by surprise. After the battle his exhausted troops refused to go farther east at the Hyphasis (Beas) River, forcing him to turn back.

**Diadochi**
The "successors," Alexander's generals who fought a series of wars over his empire after his sudden death in Babylon in 323 BCE. They included Ptolemy I Soter (Egypt), Seleucus I Nicator (who got the largest share, in Asia), Lysimachus, Antigonus, and Cassander, and the wars included the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE.

**Siege of Tyre (332 BCE)**
Alexander's seven-month siege of the Phoenician island city of Tyre. Unable to attack it normally, he built a long causeway (mole) from the mainland to bring siege towers up to its walls. He reused siege engines at Gaza, where he reportedly dragged the governor Batis behind his chariot like Achilles did with Hector.

**Cleitus the Black**
A senior officer who had saved Alexander's life at the Battle of the Granicus by cutting off the arm of the Persian Spithridates. During a drunken argument in 328 BCE, Alexander killed Cleitus with a spear, an episode told by Plutarch and Arrian.

**Philip II and Aristotle**
Alexander was the son of Philip II of Macedon, who built the Macedonian army and its long sarissa pike, and of Olympias, who belonged to a snake-handling cult. Aristotle tutored Alexander as a youth, and Alexander became king when Philip was assassinated by his bodyguard Pausanias in 336 BCE.

**Gordian Knot**
A complicated knot at Gordium in Anatolia; legend said whoever untied it would rule Asia. Alexander supposedly solved it by cutting it with his sword.

**Companion Cavalry and the hammer-and-anvil tactic**
The Companions were Alexander's elite heavy cavalry, which he often led in person. In the hammer-and-anvil tactic, the Macedonian phalanx (the anvil) pinned the enemy in place while the cavalry (the hammer) struck the flank or rear.

**Parmenion and Philotas**
Parmenion was Philip II's veteran general and Alexander's senior adviser. When Parmenion's son Philotas was accused of hiding an assassination plot, Alexander had Philotas executed and then ordered Parmenion killed as well.

**Roxana and the Sogdian Rock**
At the Sogdian Rock, a fortress in Central Asia whose defenders mocked that he would need "men with wings," Alexander's soldiers climbed the cliffs at night. He then married the Bactrian/Sogdian princess Roxana; after his death, Cassander murdered her and their son.

**Hephaestion and the Susa weddings**
Hephaestion was Alexander's closest friend, possible lover, and a top commander. At Susa in 324 BCE Alexander held mass weddings marrying his officers to Persian women, himself taking Stateira and Parysatis, while Hephaestion married Stateira's sister Drypetis. When Hephaestion died, Alexander built him an enormous funeral pyre.

**Arrian's Anabasis of Alexander**
The main surviving ancient history of Alexander's campaigns, written by Arrian of Nicomedia in the 2nd century CE using earlier sources such as Ptolemy. Other key sources are Plutarch's Life of Alexander (paired with his Life of Caesar) and Quintus Curtius Rufus.

**Alexandria and the oracle at Siwa**
Alexander founded Alexandria in Egypt, planned by the architect Dinocrates; it became the Ptolemaic capital, home to the Great Library and to the anatomist Herophilus. Alexander was declared pharaoh, and at the oracle of Zeus-Ammon at Siwa he was hailed as a son of the god.

**Mallian campaign and the Gedrosian Desert**
On his way back from India, Alexander was nearly killed by an arrow to the chest while storming a Mallian citadel, probably near Multan. He then led part of his army on a disastrous march across the Gedrosian Desert, where many soldiers died.
